name: Democritus
major_ideas: Perception and the primary/secondary quality distinction
biography: Co-founder of atomism and the chapter's more fully documented figure; worked out the theory in detail, applying it to cosmology, biology, perception, and ethics, and held a materialist, deterministic, and religiously sceptical worldview centered on cheerfulness as the goal of life. Their doctrine of the void is explicitly rejected by Aristotle in the Physics. The atomist philosopher whose physics (atoms and the void) Epicurus adopted as the foundation of his own system, while never publicly acknowledging the full extent of his debt.
central_doctrines: Perception and the primary/secondary quality distinction: Democritus's distinction between perception of the senses (dependent partly on the perceiver's sense-organs and therefore potentially deceptive) and perception of the understanding (dependent only on the object perceived); qualities like warmth, taste, and colour belong to the former and are not truly in the object, while qualities like weight, density, and hardness are truly in the object.
russell_view: Russell treats Leucippus and Democritus together as the founders of a single system, crediting Leucippus with its fundamental ideas and Democritus with their detailed elaboration. He reconstructs their theory of atoms and the void as an attempt to reconcile Parmenides's logic (that there can be no real coming-to-be, passing-away, or void) with the observed facts of motion and plurality, conceding that the atomists never logically refuted Parmenides's argument against the void but simply insisted on it as required by experience. Russell defends them against the standard ancient charge of leaving atomic motion unaccounted for, arguing any causal or theistic account faces the identical problem of an unexplained starting point. He uses the atomists' void/space problem to launch an extended historical survey (Aristotle, Newton, Descartes, Leibniz, Einstein) concluding that Einstein's physics vindicates Leibniz's relational view of space over Newton's absolute space, even though Russell judges the Newtonian view to be the strict logical descendant of the atomists' own position. Russell praises the atomists' commitment to mechanistic over teleological explanation as scientifically fruitful and contrasts it favorably with the purpose-driven thought of Socrates, Plato, and Aristotle, which he says 'led science up a blind alley' until the Renaissance. He details Democritus's materialist cosmology (many worlds, atomic vortices), his likening of warmth/taste/colour to sense-dependent qualities (compared to Locke) as against 'really' objective qualities like weight and hardness, and his ethics of cheerfulness, moderation, friendship, and preference for democracy, which Russell compares to Jeremy Bentham. Russell closes the chapter (and the pre-Socratic sequence) by calling Democritus 'the last of the Greek philosophers to be free from a certain fault which vitiated all later ancient and medieval thought': an undue emphasis on man relative to the universe, a decline he traces through the Sophists' scepticism, Socrates's turn to ethics, Plato's rejection of the sensory world, and Aristotle's belief in purpose as fundamental to science.
why_this_matters: Leucippus and Democritus founded atomism, holding that everything consists of indestructible, physically indivisible atoms moving through an empty void, differing only in shape and size. Atomism was devised to reconcile Parmenides's logical arguments against change and the void with the observed fact of motion; the atomists conceded they had no logical refutation of Parmenides and simply insisted on the void as an empirical necessity.
